cards.title: Introduction to Exceptions
cards.content: Errors in Python broadly fall into two categories: syntax errors and exceptions. Syntax errors are detected by the parser, while exceptions occur during execution even if the code is syntactically correct.

cards.title: The try-except Block
cards.content:
To catch and handle runtime errors gracefully, we use the try and except blocks.

try:
    result = 10 / 0
except ZeroDivisionError:
    print("Cannot divide by zero!")

cards.title: Else and Finally Clauses
cards.content:
The else block runs if no exceptions occur, and the finally block always executes, regardless of whether an exception occurred or not.

try:
    f = open('data.txt')
except FileNotFoundError:
    print('File not found')
else:
    print('File read successfully')
finally:
    f.close()

cards.title: Raising Exceptions
cards.content:
You can force an exception to occur using the raise keyword. This is useful for validating inputs or enforcing business logic.

def set_age(age):
    if age < 0:
        raise ValueError("Age cannot be negative")
    return age

cards.title: Creating Custom Exceptions
cards.content:
Python allows you to define your own exception classes by inheriting from the built-in Exception class.

class InsufficientFundsError(Exception):
    pass

raise InsufficientFundsError("Balance is too low")

3. else block runs if no error occurs
4. finally block runs at the very end

cards.title: Summary
cards.content:
Proper error handling makes your Python applications robust and user-friendly. Remember to:

  • Use specific except clauses.
  • Utilize else for code that depends on success.
  • Always clean up resources in finally.
  • Create custom exceptions when domain logic requires it.
